new_statements.quote: Les langues congolaises du groupe C20 disposent de deux types de tons: 1) Les tons ponctuels: a) Le ton haut (') b) Le ton bas (non marqué) Dans toutes ces langues, les deux tons assument la fonction distinctive. 2) Les tons modulés Ce sont: a) Le ton modulé montant b) Le ton modulé descendant Ils affectent les voyelles longues que nous transcrivons au moyen de deux voyelles. Toutes ces langues réalisent la combinaison des tons des deux types.
new_statements.translation: The Congolese languages of group C20 have two types of tones: 1) level tones: a) high tone (marked with an acute), b) low tone (unmarked). In all these languages the two tones have distinctive function. 2) contour tones: a) rising, b) falling; they affect long vowels, which we transcribe with two vowels. All these languages realise combinations of tones of both types.
new_statements.citation: Ndinga Oba, Antoine. 2003. Les langues bantoues du Congo-Brazzaville: étude typologique des langues du groupe C20 (mbosi ou mbochi). Tome 1: Introduction, Présentation, Phonologie. Paris: L'Harmattan.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened; PDF page 40 (liseuse image 285, printed p.279) rendered and read as an image: heading 'Inventaire général et classement / Les tons', text 'Les langues congolaises du groupe C20 disposent de deux types de tons: 1) Les tons ponctuels: a) Le ton haut (') b) Le ton bas (non marqué) Dans toutes ces langues, les deux tons assument la fonction distinctive. 2) Les tons modulés Ce sont: a) Le ton modulé montant vv b) Le ton modulé descendant vv Ils affectent les voyelles longues que nous transcrivons au moyen de deux voyelles. Toutes ces langues réalisent la combinaison des tons des deux types.' -- matches the reported quote word for word (the compiler only dropped the 'vv' tone-diagram…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Koyo, like the other six Congolese C20 languages in Ndinga Oba's survey, is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with contours on long vowels; the accessible pages say nothing about word stress or accent, and the Koyo-specific phonology chapter could not be opened.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level typological synthesis explicitly covering Koyó (C24) among Mboko, Akwa, Ngare, Mbosi, Likwala, Likuba; lexical tone on the word; no statement about stress, accent, or phrase-level prominence in the accessible pages.
new_statements.identity_note: Ndinga Oba's quoted statement is a group-level synthesis over the seven Congolese C20 languages he studied first-hand (Mboko C21, Akwa C22, Ngare C23, Koyó C24, Mbosi C25, Likwala C26, Likuba C27), explicitly including Koyó = koyo1242; it is not a Koyo-only passage. Gazania 1972 describes the Koyo of Fort-Rousset (= Owando); Okombi 2019 describes the Manga dialectal variety of Koyó. Do not confuse with 'Koyo' of South Sudan (= Lokoya, loko1255). The earlier scan's 'Pepper 1954 phonology' is in fact a text/sound-recording collection on the Kouyou (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a text collection).

new_statements.quote: For example, in a number of Northwest Bantu, Bantoid and Cross-River languages, voiceless stops are found only stem-initially (Hyman 1990, in press), e.g. Koyo /ɔ̀-tɛ́tɔ́/, /è-kúkí/ → [ɔ̀-tɛ́rɔ́] 'basket', [è-kúgí] 'door'. While such phenomena are occasionally cited as evidence for stem-initial accent, it is significant that reduplications typically produce exceptions (e.g. [ɔ̀-tɛ́tɛ́] 'spark', [ì-kákàní] 'legend'). Whether one treats these latter as having two stems with initial consonant correspondence or by some other means, if voicelessness = accent, then these words would have two (demarcative) accents. SA can have such effects, but I do not take the presence of such effects to unambiguously indicate accent.
new_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2006. Word-prosodic typology. Phonology 23(2): 225-257 (fn. 10 on Koyo stem-initial consonant strength vs. 'stem-initial accent').
new_statements.locator: fn. 10, p. 248 (PDF page 24); the only Koyo passage in the paper

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tone-language-no-stress record (Ndinga Oba 2003, p. 279: two distinctive punctual tones H/L plus modulated tones): Hyman's Koyo forms are tone-marked and he claims no stress for the language. It adds the detail that the stem-initial restriction of voiceless stops in Koyo has been read by others as evidence of a stem-initial (demarcative) accent, a reading Hyman rejects as not unambiguous; so a fixed: initial syllable (stem-initial) accent reading for Koyo is on record as a possibility but is not asserted by any source opened. The footnote's IPA was read from the rendered page scan because the PDF text garbles it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress placement is stated for Koyo. Hyman cites his own Koyo data (voiceless stops restricted to stem-initial position, tone-marked H/L forms) as the kind of positional distribution that some authors read as 'stem-initial accent', and explicitly declines to take it as unambiguous evidence of accent, noting reduplicated stems would then carry two demarcative accents. The body text on p. 248 about stem-initial stress and the tone-dependent stress algorithm (25) concerns Ayutla Mixtec (Pankratz & Pike), not Koyo.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none for Koyo (the 'two (demarcative) accents' remark is a reductio against the voicelessness = accent reading, not a claim of secondary stress)
new_statements.exceptions: Reduplicated stems [ɔ̀-tɛ́tɛ́] 'spark', [ì-kákàní] 'legend' show a stem-internal voiceless stop, i.e. exceptions to the stem-initial-only distribution that the putative stem-initial-accent reading rests on
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman's Koyo data are his own first-hand elicitations (cf. the CBOLD Koyo dictionary, Gazania & Hyman); no dialect is named. Ndinga Oba 2003 lists the language as 'C.24 Koyó' and its p. 279 tone statement covers the whole C20 (Mbochi) group, Koyo included. Kouarata 2014's 'no accentual structuring' sentence (noted in from the mbos1242 check) is about Mbochi C25 varieties, not Koyo.

tone_statements.citation: Ikemou, Régina Patience. 2018. Les processus tonals en koyó. Linguistique et Langues Africaines 4: 101-113. Villejuif: LLACAN / Éditions Lambert-Lucas. doi:10.4000/lla.11405. (Same title and abstract also issued as Revue Interdisciplinaire 1(1), 2018, revues.imist.ma, record 14601.)
tone_statements.quote: Le koyó fait usage de deux tons, haut (H) et bas (B). Bien d’autres études avant nous sont unanimes sur le nombre (deux) de tons en koyó, (p.ex. Gazania 1972, Elounga 2012). Dans cette langue, le ton a pour support la more. [...] La voyelle du préfixe de classe est de ton bas (B). [...] Les exemples ci-dessus montrent que le ton, en koyó, a une valeur distinctive. [...] En conclusion, l’on retiendra que le koyó a deux tons ponctuels : Haut et Bas. [...] La langue dispose aussi d’un ton H flottant qui n’émerge que dans un contexte syntaxique particulier (présence d’objet).
tone_statements.translation: Koyó uses two tones, high (H) and low (L). Many other studies before ours agree on the number (two) of tones in Koyó (e.g. Gazania 1972, Elounga 2012). In this language the tone-bearing unit is the mora. [...] The vowel of the class prefix is low-toned (L). [...] The examples above show that tone in Koyó has a distinctive value. [...] In conclusion, Koyó has two level tones: High and Low. [...] The language also has a floating H tone which surfaces only in a particular syntactic context (presence of an object).
tone_statements.locator: p. 103, section 1 'L'identification des tons'; last two sentences from the Conclusion, p. 111

sources.note: Two level tones H and L (only H marked), mora as TBU, tone lexically distinctive with minimal pairs; noun-root tone patterns H, HH, HB, HBH, HBB, HHB, HHH, B, BB, BH, BHB, BHH, BBB; class prefixes always L; verbal extensions toneless, receiving tone by anticipation from the final vowel; four tonal processes analysed autosegmentally: tonal stability (with compensatory lengthening), anticipatory tonal assimilation, tone drop on the class-prefix vowel, and insertion of a floating H that surfaces only before an object. No contour tones posited as units (one tone per mora); nothing on stress or ac…
